principles.name: Create the future
principles.description: Builders and inventors driven by deep empathy for customers. Look around the corner, welcome new ideas, and make bold bets real.
evidence_signals: Proposed or built something new from a customer insight, not just a request
Took a bold bet and explains how the risk was managed
Shows curiosity about where the product or technology (for example AI) is going

principles.name: Own the outcome
principles.description: Think and act like an owner. Take initiative, bias toward action, and own the end result, not just your part.
evidence_signals: Took initiative on a problem nobody assigned
Followed through after launch and fixed what broke
Talks about the business result, not only the task completed

principles.name: Raise the bar
principles.description: Aim high and play to win. Focus relentlessly on execution, celebrate excellence, and be intellectually honest about where to improve.
evidence_signals: Raised quality or performance with a measurable before and after
Admits honestly where the work fell short and what changed
Holds self and team to a high standard of execution

principles.name: Be genuine
principles.description: Be yourself, embrace and respect diversity, and support and challenge each other by being honest and direct.
evidence_signals: Included or supported people with different views or backgrounds

rounds.name: Talent partner screen
rounds.notes: Background, goals and role expectations. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Online assessment
rounds.notes: Sometimes required, mainly for early-career roles. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager screen
rounds.notes: Resume projects, technical deep dive on past decisions, ownership and impact, culture fit.

rounds.name: Coding (data structures and algorithms)
rounds.notes: Usually two rounds. Live coding. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Low-level / object-oriented design
rounds.notes: Design and code classes for a system such as an in-memory file system or rental platform. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: High-level design; senior candidates get problems grounded in Adobe products (document services, large assets, AI features).

rounds.name: Director / leadership round
rounds.notes: Behavioral and leadership questions, sometimes with a high-level design discussion.

rounds.name: Product design case
rounds.notes: Design or improve a product for a user segment; MVP scope and success metrics.

rounds.name: Analytics and metrics
rounds.notes: Subscription, trial conversion and engagement metrics; diagnosing metric changes.

rounds.name: Technical collaboration
rounds.notes: How the PM works with engineering and reasons about technical trade-offs.

question_patterns.pattern: A time the candidate improved a process or solved a problem on their own initiative
A disagreement within the team and how the candidate handled it honestly and respectfully
A time the candidate pushed work to a higher standard than required and measured the difference
How the candidate would handle a strong performer who is hurting team health or engagement
Walk through a project on the resume: architecture, obstacles, own decisions and measurable impact
How the candidate would deliver a project with far fewer people or time than estimated
Why Adobe, and how the candidate would contribute to the company's next big bets
Design a service for rich documents or large binary assets with versioning, sync and collaboration
Design a common backend component such as a cache, queue or search suggestion service and discuss scaling
Design how a generative AI feature is served to many users while balancing latency and compute cost
Adapt an existing creative or document product for a specific user segment or market
Define how to measure success for a product or feature, including subscription and engagement metrics

sample_questions.question: Give an example of a time you took the initiative to improve a process or fix a problem at work.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a problem nobody owned. Describe how you noticed it, sized the cost, and acted without waiting. Explain how you got buy-in, what you changed, and the measurable result (time saved, incidents reduced). Show follow-through after the change. Pitfall: an improvement that was really your assigned task.

looking_for: Whether you act on problems nobody owns
How you size the cost of a problem before fixing it
strong_signals: Shows how you got buy-in from others
Ends with a measured result and follow-through
watch_outs: An improvement that was really your assigned work
No numbers on what changed

sample_questions.question: How would you deal with a manager on your team who is very strong technically but has very low team engagement scores?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start by understanding, not judging: look at the feedback, talk to the manager and the team. Separate technical credibility from people leadership. Give direct, specific feedback, agree on a plan (coaching, delegation, 1:1 practice), and set check-in points with measures. Say what you would do if it does not improve. Show care for both the person and the team.

looking_for: How you coach a manager whose team is disengaged
Whether you seek to understand before you judge
strong_signals: Separates technical skill from people leadership
Sets a clear plan with check-ins and measures
watch_outs: Jumping straight to removing the manager
Ignoring how the team feels

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a disagreement in your team and how you handled it.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Choose a real disagreement with stakes. Show you understood the other view, argued with data, stayed respectful and direct, and helped the team reach a decision. Describe the outcome and the relationship afterwards. Pitfall: a story where you simply won.

looking_for: How you handle real disagreement on a team
Whether you argue with data and stay respectful
strong_signals: Explains the other view fairly
Describes the decision and the relationship afterwards
watch_outs: A story where you simply won
A disagreement with no real stakes

sample_questions.question: The estimate for a project is 9 people for 9 months, but you have 3 people and 3 months. How would you deliver it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the real goal and the must-have outcome. Cut scope to an MVP, sequence by risk and value, and reuse existing components or buy where possible. Be explicit about what you drop and the quality bar you keep. Negotiate with stakeholders openly and set checkpoints. Show judgment, not heroics. Pitfall: promising everything by working nights.

looking_for: How you deliver under hard limits on people and time
Whether you cut scope with judgment, not heroics
strong_signals: Defines the must-have outcome and an MVP
Says openly what gets dropped and keeps a quality bar
watch_outs: Promising everything by working nights
Not involving stakeholders in the trade-offs

sample_questions.question: What do you think Adobe's big future bets are, and how would you help with them in this role?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Show real research: for example generative AI in creative and document products, cloud collaboration, and digital experience. Link one bet to the team you would join and to your concrete skills. Offer one thoughtful idea or question. Pitfall: generic praise of the brand.

looking_for: Whether you have researched where the company is heading
How you connect its bets to your own skills
strong_signals: Links one specific bet to the team you would join
Offers a thoughtful idea or question
watch_outs: Generic praise of the brand
Naming bets with no link to your role

sample_questions.question: Describe a past project you are proud of.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a project at the scope of the target level. Explain the problem, your role, two key decisions with trade-offs, and measurable impact for users or the business. Be ready for deep technical follow-ups on the architecture. Say what you would do differently.

looking_for: The depth and scope of your past work
How you make and explain key decisions
strong_signals: Covers two decisions with their trade-offs
Gives measurable impact and what you would change
watch_outs: A project below the level you are applying for
Not being ready for deep technical follow-ups

sample_questions.question: Explain the architecture of your current project and the main obstacles you have faced in your role.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give a short system overview with the main components and data flow. Pick one or two real obstacles (technical or organizational), what you did, and the outcome. Show you understand why the system is built as it is. Pitfall: blaming others for obstacles.

looking_for: Whether you understand why your system is built as it is
How you deal with real obstacles
strong_signals: Gives a short, clear overview of components and data flow
Describes what you did about an obstacle and the result
watch_outs: Getting lost in detail before the big picture
Blaming others for obstacles

sample_questions.question: Why do you want to join Adobe?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Connect a specific product or technology area to your experience and goals. Mention what you would bring in the first months. Be genuine; Adobe's own interview tips stress real interest in the products and curious questions.

looking_for: Whether your interest in the company is genuine
How your experience fits a specific product area
strong_signals: Names a specific product or technology you care about
Says what you would bring in your first months
watch_outs: An answer that fits any company
Talking only about perks or prestige

sample_questions.question: Design a cloud document service for files with complex internal structure such as layers and embedded assets, supporting version history, sync across devices and collaborative editing.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify document sizes, users per document and offline needs. Model the document as a tree of components so changes are small deltas. Store large assets separately (object storage, content-addressed chunks). Version with an operation log plus periodic snapshots. Sync deltas, and choose a conflict strategy (OT, CRDT, or per-component locking) with reasons. Cover permissions, undo, and storage cost. Pitfall: re-uploading whole files on every change.

looking_for: How you model a complex document for sync and versioning
How you choose a conflict strategy for collaboration
strong_signals: Treats changes as small deltas, not whole files
Keeps large assets apart from document structure
Explains the trade-offs of the conflict approach
watch_outs: Re-uploading the whole file on every change
Skipping permissions, undo or storage cost

sample_questions.question: Design a pipeline to store and deliver very large binary creative assets to users around the world.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover chunked, resumable uploads, content hashing and dedup, object storage with lifecycle tiers, metadata store, thumbnail and preview generation jobs, CDN delivery with cache keys and invalidation, and delta sync for edits. Discuss cost versus latency and regional replication. Strong answers quantify sizes and bandwidth.

looking_for: How you move very large files reliably around the world
How you balance cost against latency
strong_signals: Covers resumable chunked uploads and deduplication
Puts numbers on file sizes and bandwidth
Plans CDN caching and invalidation
watch_outs: Treating huge files like small API payloads
No plan for edits or regional copies

sample_questions.question: Design the backend for a generative AI image feature used inside a creative app at large scale.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify latency targets and request volume. Describe a request gateway, queueing, GPU inference pool with autoscaling and batching, result storage and delivery. Cover quotas and entitlement checks, content safety filtering, caching repeated prompts, and graceful degradation. The key trade-off is interactive latency versus GPU cost; state how you balance it and what you would measure.

looking_for: How you serve an expensive model at large scale
How you trade interactive latency against GPU cost
strong_signals: Covers queueing, batching and autoscaling of inference
Includes quotas, safety filtering and graceful degradation
watch_outs: Ignoring cost or capacity limits
No content safety or entitlement checks

sample_questions.question: Design a typeahead search box that suggests completions as the user types.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Requirements: latency budget per keystroke, ranking by popularity, personalization, freshness. Data structure: prefix trie or precomputed top-k per prefix. Serving: in-memory shards, client debouncing, caching common prefixes. Offline pipeline to rebuild counts from logs. Discuss trade-offs of freshness versus cost and how to filter bad suggestions.

looking_for: How you meet a tight latency budget per keystroke
Your choice of data structure for prefix lookups
strong_signals: Explains ranking, freshness and how counts get rebuilt
Uses caching and client debouncing to cut load
watch_outs: Querying a database on every keystroke
No plan to filter bad suggestions

sample_questions.question: Design a message queue for communication between services.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify delivery guarantees (at-least-once, ordering per key), throughput and retention. Describe producers, partitioned append-only logs, consumer groups with offsets, replication and leader election, acknowledgments and retries, dead-letter handling. Discuss back-pressure and the trade-off between durability and latency.

looking_for: Whether you clarify delivery and ordering guarantees first
How you design for durability and throughput
strong_signals: Covers partitions, consumer offsets and replication
Handles retries, dead letters and back-pressure
watch_outs: Vague about at-least-once versus exactly-once
No answer for a node failure

sample_questions.question: Design a caching layer that runs across multiple nodes.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover consistent hashing for key placement, replication for hot keys, eviction policy, TTLs, and invalidation on writes (write-through, write-behind or cache-aside) with consistency trade-offs. Discuss node failure and rebalancing, thundering herd protection, and metrics such as hit rate.

looking_for: How you spread keys across nodes
How you keep the cache consistent with the source of truth
strong_signals: Explains consistent hashing and rebalancing
Chooses an invalidation strategy and states its trade-off
Protects against hot keys and thundering herds
watch_outs: Ignoring what happens when a node fails
No metrics such as hit rate

sample_questions.question: Design a warehouse management system where storage spaces are rented to different firms and orders for their stored items must be processed efficiently.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify entities (warehouse, space, firm, item, order) and the key operations. Model data and APIs, then the allocation strategy for spaces (fit, fragmentation) and order processing flow with concurrency control. Discuss scale, consistency for inventory counts, and extensibility. A reported pitfall is weak structure; break the problem into components early.

looking_for: How you break an open-ended system into components
How you model entities and core operations
strong_signals: Defines the data model and APIs early
Handles concurrency on inventory and allocation
watch_outs: Weak structure that jumps between topics
Skipping consistency of stock counts

sample_questions.question: How would you position Creative Cloud to win small businesses in a specific Asian market such as Singapore?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify goal (new subscribers, revenue). Segment small businesses by need (social content, print, web). Size the opportunity roughly. Identify barriers: price, skills, local payment, competition from simpler tools. Propose a focused offer (templates, simpler app, bundles, partners) and a go-to-market. Define metrics: trial starts, conversion, retention. Recommend one path with risks.

looking_for: How you frame a go-to-market problem in a new market
Whether you segment customers by need
strong_signals: Sizes the opportunity roughly and names local barriers
Recommends one focused path with metrics and risks
watch_outs: A generic plan that ignores the local market
No clear goal or success metric

sample_questions.question: How would you measure the success of a short-video feature in a social app?
sample_questions.strong_answer: State the feature goal first. Pick a north star (for example time spent watching or creators posting weekly) and supporting metrics for creators, viewers and the business. Add guardrails such as impact on other surfaces. Explain how to attribute change (experiments, cohorts). Pitfall: a long list of metrics with no hierarchy.

looking_for: Whether you start from the feature's goal
How you build a hierarchy of metrics
strong_signals: Picks a clear north star with supporting metrics
Adds guardrails and a way to attribute change
watch_outs: A long list of metrics with no priority
Ignoring creators or the wider app

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Member of Technical Staff 1. Delivers well-defined tasks with guidance.
Member of Technical Staff 2. Owns features independently inside one team.
Owns components or services end to end, leads designs and mentors engineers.
Technical lead for a product area; drives architecture across teams.
Sets technical direction for a large product or platform and influences the organization.
Owns a product area, its roadmap and metrics, and leads cross-functional teams.

persona.tone: Professional and friendly, relationship-driven, genuinely curious about the candidate's work
persona.pace: Moderate; moves quickly through resume topics then goes deep on one project
persona.pushback_style: Probes trade-offs behind technical decisions and asks for measurable impact; may shift requirements mid-design
persona.closing_style: Invites thoughtful questions about the team and products

case_style.notes: PM cases center on improving Adobe products for a segment (SMB, new markets) and on subscription and engagement metrics. Estimation is light.

sources.title: Evolving Adobe's values and culture (Adobe blog)
Get a job at Adobe: interview process and top questions
What to expect in the Adobe system design interview
Adobe product manager interview guide (Interview Query)

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: Adobe has no dedicated values round; values are probed inside hiring manager and leadership rounds. Adobe's careers page still mentions the older values (genuine, exceptional, innovative, involved), so interviewers may use either set.
loop_structure: rounds vary widely by team and country; many India candidate reports show 2 DSA + LLD + HM/director rounds. PM loop comes from third-party guides only.
bar_by_level: Adobe does not publish its ladder; title-to-level mapping comes from third-party summaries, and US postings also use Software Engineer / Senior Software Engineer titles.
persona: based on Adobe's 'relationship-driven' interview tips and candidate reports; thin evidence.
scoring_weights: estimated; no public source gives weights.
case_style: PM case examples come from third-party guides (one example uses a non-Adobe product).
